'''Hans Charles Freeman''' [[Order of Australia|AM]], [[Australian Academy of Science|FAA]] (26 May 1929 – 9 November 2008) was a German-born Australian [[bioinorganic chemistry|bioinorganic chemist]], protein crystallographer, and professor of [[inorganic chemistry]] who spent most of his academic career at the [[University of Sydney]].<ref name = "Guss_IUCr">{{cite journal|title= Obituary: Hans C. Freeman (1929–2008)|first1= M.|last1= Guss|journal= [[International Union of Crystallography|International Union of Crystallography Newsletter]]|volume= 17|issue= 2|year= 2009|url= http://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-17/number-2/hans-c.-freeman|access-date= 29 July 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180121184449/http://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-17/number-2/hans-c.-freeman|archive-date= 21 January 2018|url-status= live}}</ref> His best known contributions to [[chemistry]] were his work explaining the unusual [[chemical structure|structural]], [[electrochemistry|electrochemical]], and [[spectroscopy|spectroscopic]] properties of blue [[copper proteins]], particularly [[plastocyanin]].<ref name = "Hambley_JBIC" /> He also introduced [[protein crystallography]] to Australia<ref name = "SMH_obit" /> and was a strong advocate for courses to ensure Australian scientists have good access to [[Big Science|"big science"]] facilities.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> Freeman has received numerous honours, including being elected a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] (FAA)<ref name = "FAA" /> and appointed a Member of the [[Order of Australia]] (AM)<ref name = "AM" /> by the [[Australian Government]].  He was a charismatic lecturer who voluntarily continued teaching well into his formal retirement and imbued his students with a love of science.<ref name = "Guss_IUCr" />

==Early years and education==
Hans Charles Freeman was the first and only son of Karl and Lotte Freeman and was born in [[Breslau]] in Germany in 1929<ref name = "SMH_obit" /> (now [[Wrocław]], Poland).<ref name = Breslau>{{cite book|chapter = A Note on Names|pages = xi-xii|title = Uprooted: How Breslau Became Wroclaw during the Century of Expulsions|first = Gregor|last = Thum|authorlink = Gregor Thum|publisher = [[Princeton University Press]]|year = 2011|isbn = 9781400839964|chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=D3IDT1RmI38C&pg=PR11|quote = [W]hen German Breslau was ceded to Poland [in 1945] ... the city name became a politically sensitive issue.  ... This changed in 1990, however.  With the definitive recognition of Poland's western border by a reunified Germany and the ensuing German-Polish reconciliation, Wroclaw's city name soon ceased to be a political issue. While people no longer question that "Wroclaw" is the only official name today, the use of "Breslau" within the German language is fully accepted.}}</ref> In 1938, following a tip-off from a [[Nazi]] party member, Karl decided to relocate his Jewish family to Australia.  Karl brought his knowledge of [[detergent]]s (a novelty in Australia at the time) to his new homeland, applying it to the problem of cleaning blood-stained blankets that would otherwise be wasted.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> After the war, he founded K. H. Freeman Pty Ltd, a detergent and soap manufacturing company; Hans spent many weekends working in the factory, gaining a practical insight into chemistry.<ref name = "SMH_obit" />

Hans adapted well to his new environment, quickly mastering his new language and demonstrating his outstanding scholastic ability.  He was [[Dux#Education|dux]] of his primary school, dux of [[Sydney Boys High]] in 1945,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.shsobu.org.au/wp-content/uploads/professors.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190323090429/http://www.shsobu.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professors.pdf |archive-date=23 March 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> and took his [[bachelor's degree]] with the [[University Medal#Australia|university medal]] in chemistry in 1949.<ref name = "SMH_obit">{{Cite news|last = Stephens|first = T.|title = From riches to rags to protein pioneer|newspaper = The Sydney Morning Herald|location = Sydney|date = 5 December 2008|url = http://www.smh.com.au/news/obituaries/from-riches-to-rags-to-protein-pioneer/2008/12/04/1228257223616.html|access-date = 30 July 2010|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150924202840/http://www.smh.com.au/news/obituaries/from-riches-to-rags-to-protein-pioneer/2008/12/04/1228257223616.html|archive-date = 24 September 2015|url-status = live}}</ref> He was one of the ten chemistry students in his class at Sydney Boys High to go on to become Professors of Chemistry.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> After receiving his [[Master of Science|MSc]] in 1952 under the supervision of [[Raymond Le Fèvre]] [[Royal Society#Fellows|FRS]], Freeman attended [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] on a [[Rotary Foundation]] Fellowship where, at the urging of [[Linus Pauling]], he learned the fundamentals of [[crystallography]].<ref name = "Hambley_JBIC">{{cite journal|year=2009|title=Hans Freeman 1929–2008|last1=Hambley|first1=T.|journal=[[Journal of Biological Inorganic Chemistry|J. Biol. Inorg. Chem.]]|volume=14|issue=3|pages=327–328|doi=10.1007/s00775-009-0484-x|s2cid=37059316|doi-access=free}}</ref> He received a [[PhD]] in 1957 for his work on the structure of [[biuret|biuret hydrate]],<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1038/184707a0|year=1959|title=Crystallographic Studies of the Biuret Reaction|last1=Freeman|first1=H. C.|last2=Smith|first2=J. E. W. L.|last3=Taylor|first3=J. C.|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=184|issue=4687|pages=707–710|pmid=13824733|bibcode = 1959Natur.184..707F |s2cid=4178061}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1107/S0365110X61001194|year=1961|title=The Crystal Structure of Biuret Hydrate|last1=Hughes|first1=E. W.|last2=Yakel|first2=H. L.|last3=Freeman|first3=H. C.|journal=[[Acta Crystallographica|Acta Crystallogr.]]|volume=14|issue=4|pages=345–352|doi-access=free|bibcode=1961AcCry..14..345H }}</ref> where he completed most of the calculations for the crystal structure by hand.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" />

==Personal life==
Freeman came to Australia with his parents and his sister, Eva.  Following the death of his father in 1958, he became a Director of K. H. Freeman Pty Ltd, which continues to operate today. He met Edith Siou in 1964 and they married in 1966. They have two children, Maeva and Philip.<ref name="SMH_obit" />

==Career==
[[File:PDB 1plc EBI.jpg|thumb|right|Structure of poplar plastocyanin<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Guss|first1= J. M.|last2= Bartunik|first2= H. D.|last3= Freeman|first3= H. C.|title= Accuracy and Precision in Protein Structure Analysis: Restrained Least-Squares Refinement of the Structure of Poplar Plastocyanin at 1.33 Å Resolution|journal= [[Acta Crystallographica|Acta Crystallogr. B]] |volume= 48|issue= 6|pages= 790–811|year=1992 |doi= 10.1107/S0108768192004270 |pmid=1492962|bibcode= 1992AcCrB..48..790G}}</ref>]]
Freeman was appointed to the faculty of the [[University of Sydney]] in 1954 as a Lecturer, working his way up until he was made the inaugural Professor of Inorganic Chemistry in 1971.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> Freeman pioneered the use of computers in crystallography in Australia, working on [[SILLIAC]] (the Australian cousin of the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois]]' [[ILLIAC]] machine and Australia's second computer) after its installation in 1956.  His research group extended its interests beyond purely [[organic compound]]s and on to [[metal complex]]es (such as copper biuret, one of the first bioinorganic substances to be structurally determined<ref name = "Hambley_JBIC" />) and went on to determine the structures of numerous metal complexes of [[amino acid]]s and [[peptide]]s.<ref name = "Guss_obit">{{cite journal|year=2009|title=Hans C. Freeman (1929–2009) Obituary|last1=Guss|first1=J. M.|journal=[[Acta Crystallographica|Acta Crystallogr. D]]|volume=65|issue=1|pages=93–95|doi=10.1107/S0907444908041565|pmid=19153471|doi-access=free}}</ref>

[[File:Plastocyanin copper binding.png|thumb|left|The copper site in plastocyanin, with the four amino acids that bind the metal labelled]]
In 1970, the focus of Freeman's research became [[X-ray crystallography#Biological macromolecular crystallography|protein crystallography]] and he turned his attention to the blue [[copper proteins]] (cupredoxins) and particularly the electron transport protein [[plastocyanin]].  The intensely blue colour of plastocyanin and its unusual [[redox]] properties had frustrated all attempts to synthesise a small molecule mimic.<ref name ="Guss_obit" /> It was not until 1977 that his group finally determined the structure of plastocyanin crystallised from the [[poplar tree]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Chapman|first1= G. V.|last2= Colman|first2= P. M.|authorlink2= Peter Colman|last3= Freeman|first3= H. C.|last4= Guss|first4= J. M.|last5= Murata|first5= M.|last6= Norris|first6= V. A.|last7= Ramshaw|first7= J. A. M.|last8= Venkatappa|first8= M. P.|title= Preliminary Crystallographic Data for a Copper-Containing Protein, Plastocyanin|journal= [[Journal of Molecular Biology|J. Mol. Biol.]]|volume= 110|issue= 1|pages= 187–189|year= 1977|doi= 10.1016/S0022-2836(77)80106-X|pmid= 845945}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1= Colman|first1= P. M.|authorlink1= Peter Colman|last2= Freeman|first2= H. C.|last3= Guss|first3= J. M.|last4= Murata|first4= M.|last5= Norris|first5= V. A.|last6= Ramshaw|first6= J. A. M.|last7= Venkatappa|first7= M. P.|title= X-Ray Crystal Structure Analysis of Plastocyanin at 2.7 Å Resolution|journal= [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume= 272|issue= 5651|pages= 319–324|year= 1978|doi= 10.1038/272319a0|bibcode = 1978Natur.272..319C |s2cid= 4226644}}</ref> (see diagram at right); this was the first protein crystal structure determined in the [[Southern Hemisphere]].<ref name ="Craig_Medal" /> Together with subsequent work in collaboration with [[Edward I. Solomon|Ed Solomon]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Penfield|first1= K. W.|last2= Gay|first2= R. R.|last3= Himmelwright|first3= R. S.|last4= Eickman|first4= N. C.|last5= Norris|first5= V. A.|last6= Freeman|first6= H. C.|last7= Solomon|first7= E. I.|authorlink7= Edward I. Solomon|title= Spectroscopic Studies on Plastocyanin Single-Crystals: A Detailed Electronic-Structure Determination of the Blue Copper Active-Site|journal= [[J. Am. Chem. Soc.]] |volume= 103|issue= 15|pages= 4382–4388|year= 1981|doi= 10.1021/ja00405a016|bibcode= 1981JAChS.103.4382P}}</ref> this work led to understanding of the unusual geometry of the copper metal site (see diagram at left) as well as the [[spectroscopy|spectroscopic]] and [[electrochemistry|electrochemical]] properties characteristic of blue copper proteins.<ref name = "Hambley_JBIC" />

Later in his career, Freeman developed an interest in the applications of [[Extended X-ray absorption fine structure|EXAFS]] spectroscopy to metalloprotein structure, collaborating with both [[James Penner-Hahn]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Scott|first1= R. A.|last2= Hahn|first2= J. E.|authorlink2= James Penner-Hahn|last3= Doniach|first3= S.|last4= Freeman|first4= H. C.|last5= Hodgson|first5= K. O.|authorlink5= Keith Hodgson|title= Polarized X-Ray Absorption Spectra of Oriented Plastocyanin Single Crystals. Investigation of Methionine-Copper Coordination|journal= [[J. Am. Chem. Soc.]]|volume= 104|issue= 20|pages= 5364–5369|year= 1982|doi= 10.1021/ja00384a020|bibcode= 1982JAChS.104.5364S}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1= Penner-Hahn|first1= J. E.|authorlink1= James Penner-Hahn|last2= Murata|first2= M.|last3= Hodgson|first3= K. O.|last4= Freeman|first4= H. C.|authorlink3= Keith Hodgson|title= Low-Temperature X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy of Plastocyanin: Evidence for Copper-Site Photoreduction at Cryogenic Temperatures|journal= [[Inorganic Chemistry (journal)|Inorg. Chem.]]|volume= 28|issue= 10|pages= 1826–1832|year= 1989|doi= 10.1021/ic00309a015}}</ref> and [[Keith Hodgson]].<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> Working together, the Freeman and Hodgson groups were, in 1988, the first to determine a new crystal structure of a protein using the [[Multi-wavelength anomalous dispersion|multiple wavelength anomalous dispersion (MAD) method]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Guss|first1= J. M.|last2= Merritt|first2= E. A.|last3= Phizackerley|first3= R. P.|last4= Hedman|first4= B.|last5= Murata|first5= M.|last6= Hodgson|first6= K. O.|authorlink6= Keith Hodgson|last7= Freeman|first7= H. C.|title= Phase Determination by Multiple-Wavelength X-ray Diffraction: Crystal Structure of a Basic "Blue" Copper Protein from Cucumbers|journal= [[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume= 241|issue= 4867|pages= 806–811|year= 1988|doi= 10.1126/science.3406739|pmid= 3406739|bibcode= 1988Sci...241..806G|jstor= 1702012}} {{subscription required}}</ref>

Throughout his career, Freeman was concerned about the influence of the tyranny of distance<ref>The phrase "the tyranny of distance" comes from the 1966 book ''[[The Tyranny of Distance: How Distance Shaped Australia's History]]'' by [[Geoffrey Blainey]]</ref> on the development of Australian science.  For this reason, in 1972 Freeman and [[Alexander Boden]] [[Order of Australia|AO]], FAA, founded the Foundation for Inorganic Chemistry at the university to bring international scholars to the department to deliver a course for graduate students and give seminars for faculty.<ref name = "Guss_IUCr" /> The inaugural Foundation scholar was nobel laureate [[Linus Pauling]]<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.science.org.au/fellows/memoirs/boden.html|title= Biographical Memoirs: Alexander Boden 1913–1993|work= [[Australian Academy of Science|science.org.au]]|access-date= 8 August 2010|url-status= dead|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100502194648/http://www.science.org.au/fellows/memoirs/boden.html|archive-date= 2 May 2010}}</ref> and the Foundation has brought many other eminent research chemists to Australia.  The Foundation has thus functioned to increase Australian awareness of state of the art international research, increased international recognition of Australian research, and allowed graduate students to interact with leading chemists based in institutions far from Australia.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> Many of the students have gone on to [[Postgraduate education|post-graduate]] or [[Postdoctoral research|post-doctoral]] positions with a Foundation scholar.<ref name = "Guss_obit" />

Freeman also provided advice to the [[Government of Australia|Australian Government]] on the problem of access to "[[big science]]" facilities.  This included making major contributions to the report ''Small Country - Big Science''<ref>{{cite book|author= Australian Science and Technology Council|authorlink= Australian Science, Technology and Engineering Council|title= Small Country - Big Science: A Report to the Prime Minister on Australian Participation in Major International Accelerator and Beam Facilities|url= http://catalogue.nla.gov.au/Record/1831716|year= 1990|publisher= Australian Government Publishing Service|isbn= 0-644-11982-9|access-date= 8 August 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110614011642/http://catalogue.nla.gov.au/Record/1831716|archive-date= 14 June 2011|url-status= live}}</ref> in his work for the [[Australian Science, Technology and Engineering Council|Australian Science and Technology Council]].<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> The report emphasised the need for Australian researchers to have access to facilities such as [[synchrotron]] X-ray and high intensity [[neutron source]]s, and led directly to the formation of the Australian Synchrotron Research Programme (ASRP) to fund access to such facilities.  Freeman served as a board member of the ASRP until its functions were subsumed under the newly commissioned [[Australian Synchrotron]] in 2008.<ref name = "Guss_obit" /> The Australian expertise developed as a consequence of ASRP-supported research led to the Australian Synchrotron being built a decade sooner than would have otherwise been the case.<ref name = "Hambley_JBIC" />

Freeman retired from his [[Chair (academic)|Chair]] in 1997, and was succeeded by [[Leonard Francis Lindoy|Len Lindoy]] FAA.  Nevertheless, he continued working in research and became [[Emeritus Professor]] of Chemistry and Emeritus Professor of Molecular and Microbial Biosciences.  He also voluntarily continued teaching at first-year level.<ref name = "SMH_obit" /> His lecturing was described as "charismatic" and "teaching was a love and a privilege and never an obligation" for him.<ref name = "Guss_IUCr" />

==Legacy==
Freeman was principally responsible for the establishment of [[structural biology]] as a discipline in Australia.<ref name = "AM" /> He founded the first protein crystallography laboratory in Australia; by the time of his death, there were at least 15 active research groups carrying out protein crystallography in Australia and New Zealand.<ref name = "Guss_obit" /> Many former members of the Freeman research group have moved on to join one of these other groups.<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem" /> The groups interact through the Society of Crystallographers of Australia and New Zealand (SCANZ); Freeman was instrumental in forming the organisation (then called the Society of Crystallographers of Australia) in 1976, and was its Foundation President.<ref name = "Guss_IUCr" /> Working as a crystallographer, Freeman's major legacies are the understanding of plastocyanin and other blue copper proteins, and development of the MAD method as an extension of EXAFS spectroscopy.  Freeman's work in ensuring Australian scientists have access to "big science" facilities will continue to assist researchers into the future.  His teaching also leaves a legacy of "generations of students imbued with a love of science".<ref name = "Guss_IUCr" />

==Honours and awards==
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Member of the order of aust.jpg|thumb|right|The insigna for Members of the Order of Australia (AM)]] -->
Freeman was recognised for his professional achievements with Fellowships in the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] (RACI) in 1968, the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 1984,<ref name = "Hambley_AustJChem">{{cite journal|year=1995|title=Hans C. Freeman|last1=Hambley|first1=T.|journal=[[Aust. J. Chem.]]|volume=48|issue=4|pages=697–699|doi=10.1071/CH9950697}}</ref> and the [[Australian Academy of Science]] in 1984.<ref name = "FAA">{{cite web|url=http://www.science.org.au/fellows/deceased.html#f|title=Australian Academy of Science - Deceased Fellows and Memoirs|work=[[Australian Academy of Science|science.org.au]]|access-date=6 August 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111027204804/http://www.science.org.au/fellows/deceased.html#f|archive-date=27 October 2011|url-status=live}}</ref> Freeman's contributions were also recognised by the [[Government of Australia|Australian Government]] with a [[Centenary Medal]] in 2001 for "service to Australian society and science in chemistry"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1127327|title=FREEMAN, Hans Charles: Centenary Medal|work=[[Orders, decorations, and medals of Australia|itsanhonour.gov.au]]|access-date=30 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629130137/http://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/honour_roll/search.cfm?aus_award_id=1127327&search_type=quick&showInd=true|archive-date=29 June 2011|url-status=live}}</ref> and with his appointment as a Member of the [[Order of Australia]] in June 2005 for "service to science and scientific research in the field of bio-inorganic chemistry, particularly through the establishment and development of the discipline of crystallography in Australia".<ref name = "AM">{{cite web|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1135946|title=FREEMAN, Hans Charles: Member of the Order of Australia|work=[[Orders, decorations, and medals of Australia|itsanhonour.gov.au]]|access-date=6 October 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629132605/http://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/honour_roll/search.cfm?aus_award_id=1135946&search_type=simple&showInd=true|archive-date=29 June 2011|url-status=live}}</ref>

Freeman received numerous awards over his long career.  In 1980, Freeman received the Burrows Award, the premier award of the Inorganic Chemistry Division of the RACI.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.raci.org.au/page/Divisions/Inorganic-Chemistry/Inorganic-Chemistry-Awards.htm|title=Inorganic Chemistry Awards|publisher=[[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]|website=[[raci.org.au]]|access-date= 30 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100804060334/http://www.raci.org.au/page/Divisions/Inorganic-Chemistry/Inorganic-Chemistry-Awards.htm <!--Added by H3llBot-->|archive-date=4 August 2010}}</ref> He was also awarded the 1999 Leighton Memorial Medal<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.raci.org.au/page/Awards/Past-Award-Winners.htm#leighton|title=Past Award Winners - Leighton Memorial Medal|publisher=[[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]|website=[[raci.org.au]]|access-date= 30 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100715004607/http://www.raci.org.au/page/Awards/Past-Award-Winners.htm <!--Added by H3llBot-->|archive-date=15 July 2010}}</ref> which is "the RACI's most prestigious medal and is awarded in recognition of eminent services to chemistry in Australia in the broadest sense."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.raci.org.au/site/1/common/Leighton2009%20Medal.pdf|title=Leighton Medal|publisher=[[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]|website=[[raci.org.au]]|access-date=30 July 2010}}{{dead link|date=October 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> In 2007, he received both the Australian Academy of Science's Craig Medal<ref name="Craig_Medal">{{cite web|url=http://www.science.org.au/awards/awardees/2007awards.html|title=2007 Awards|work=[[Australian Academy of Science|science.org.au]]|access-date=30 July 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100427071057/http://www.science.org.au/awards/awardees/2007awards.html|archive-date=27 April 2010}}</ref> and an RACI Distinguished Fellowship.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.raci.org.au/site/1/common/Distinguished2009%20Fellowship.pdf|title=Distinguished Fellowship|publisher=[[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]|website=[[raci.org.au]]|access-date=30 July 2010}}{{dead link|date=October 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.raci.org.au/page/Awards/Past-Award-Winners.htm#distinguishedfellowship|title=Past Award Winners - Distinguished Fellowship|publisher=[[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]|website=[[raci.org.au]]|access-date= 30 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100715004607/http://www.raci.org.au/page/Awards/Past-Award-Winners.htm <!--Added by H3llBot-->|archive-date=15 July 2010}}</ref>
